sentences.text: Revenue (net interest income plus noninterest income) grew from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was a step change, not a compounder: revenue was $22.7 billion in FY2021, jumped 15.8% in FY2023 to $28.0 billion, and has grown only 1.9% since [D117][D169][D219][D189].
The FY2023 step came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, which lifted net interest income 18.1% [D184][P33].
FY2025 was a recovery year: net income rose 20.2% to $7.6 billion as noninterest expense fell 2.0% on prior-year merger and FDIC charges rolling off [F30][D227][D238][P10].
Consumer and Business Banking is still the largest segment at 31.0% of revenue in FY2025, but it shrank 3.9% and subtracted 1.3pp from growth [D251][D252][D253].
That decline came from deposit mix and second-quarter loan sales cutting net interest income 4.9% [P6].
Payment Services was the offset, adding 1.4pp on 5.4% growth to 25.8% of revenue [D260][D261][D259].
Payment Services net revenue rose on higher loan balances and lower funding costs, plus merchant processing and card volume [P4].
Profit outran revenue: net income grew 20.2% against 4.4% revenue growth, and EPS rose 21.9% with the diluted share count down 0.2% [D227][D239][D229][D237].
The efficiency ratio was 59.0% in FY2025, just below its 59.3% window median and far off the 67.4% FY2023 high [D220][D277][D276].
That is 14th percentile against seven bank peers whose median is 61.7% [D280][D281].
The FY2023 spike to 67.4% came from merger and integration charges, MUB operating costs and a $734 million FDIC special assessment [D170][P30].
The FY2025 improvement reflects those prior-year charges not repeating and lower compensation from operational efficiencies [P10].
Credit costs stayed heavy at 7.7% of revenue versus a 6.1% peer median, though the provision fell 2.3% on improved credit quality [D221][D285][P12].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; capital return is the better test [F60].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.7 billion covered only 48% of FY2025 net income, down from $7.0 billion in FY2019 [D218][F30][D65].
Buybacks collapsed from $4.5 billion in FY2019 to $489 million in FY2025, while dividends rose to $3.2 billion [X79][X85][X95].
Return on average equity was 12.2% in FY2025, above the 11.8% peer median and 71st percentile of seven banks [D226][D283][D282].
Equity grew 11.3% to $65.2 billion, the fastest pace in the window, lifting the equity-to-assets ratio to 9.4% [F114][D233][F90].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits, down from 80.5% in FY2016, and the allowance held at 2.0% of loans [D224][D10][D225].
The balance sheet looks conservatively funded, but the thin buyback means capital is accumulating rather than being returned [D218][D65].
Revenue fell 2.4% in FY2024, the only decline in the window, as net interest income dropped 6.4% [D214][D209].
The filings attribute that to higher interest rates pressuring deposit mix and pricing [P20].
It proved short-lived: revenue rebounded 4.4% in FY2025, so the flag is one period, not a trend [D239].
More persistent is the weak capital return, with buybacks at $489 million against $4.5 billion in FY2019 [X85][X79].
Efficiency ratio: a move back above the 59.3% window median would reverse the FY2025 cost improvement, visible in the FY2026 10-K [D277][D220].
Consumer and Business Banking revenue: another decline from the FY2025 level would confirm the deposit-mix drag is structural [D252][S57].
Buybacks: a figure above the FY2025 $489 million would signal capital return normalizing toward the FY2019 $4.5 billion pace [X85][X79].
